title: The Secret of String Pool
concept: String literals are stored in the String Pool and reused.

steps.title: Creating a String from a literal
steps.explanation:
**What is String Pool?**
This is a ‘recycling center’ that collects frequently used strings.
To save memory, Java creates and shares only one identical string literal.

**What is Literal?**
These refer to values (`"hello"`) typed directly into the code.
steps.keyInsight: If you create it with quotation marks (""), it will be stored in the Pool.

steps.title: Reusing the same literal
steps.explanation:
Are you trying to make “hello” again?
The JVM searches the Pool and asks, “Huh? Is there something you created earlier?” and reuse the **existing address**.
So `b` also points to the same **Pool:0x100** as `a`.

**Flyweight Pattern:**
It is a design pattern that saves memory by sharing identical objects rather than creating many.
String Pool is this pattern.

steps.title: == Comparison between literals
steps.explanation:
Since `a` and `b` point to the **same address**, the result of `==` (address comparison) is **true**.
But be careful! This is not because the strings are the same, but because they **coincidentally share the same object**.
steps.keyInsight: == is true between literals (but .equals is recommended)

javaMemoryState.warning: Literals return true with ==! But you shouldn't rely on this

steps.title: Create String with new
steps.explanation:
The `new` keyword is a command that says **“Don’t recycle, just give us a new one!”**
It doesn't care whether "hello" is in the Pool or not, it creates a new object in the regular **Heap** area.

**Heap String vs Pooled String:**
- `new`: My own private object (reusable
- `"..."`: public object (reuse O)
steps.keyInsight: new = refuse recycling, unconditionally new object

steps.title: Literal vs new comparison
steps.explanation:
`a` is from the recycling center (Pool),
`c` is a new product freshly released from the factory (Heap).
Since our origins are different, our addresses are also different.

steps.title: Register Pool with intern()
steps.explanation:
The `intern()` method requests **“Please join me in that Pool too”**.
Eventually, `d` will have the same address as `a`.
steps.keyInsight: intern() = Convert Heap string to Pool address

steps.title: Compare intern() results
steps.explanation:
`a` and `d` now point to the same Pool object.
`true`!

**Practical Tip:**
When you have to deal with millions of duplicate strings, using `intern()` can dramatically reduce memory.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of String Pool?
quiz.explanation: Saves memory by creating only one object even if you use the same string literal multiple times.

misconceptions.wrong: Strings can always be compared with ==.
misconceptions.correct: For string comparison, you must always use `.equals()`.
misconceptions.why: For literals, `==` might work with luck because of the Pool, but strings read from user input or files will be treated like `new` objects and `==` will fail.

misconceptions.wrong: String Pool is not emptied even if memory is full.
misconceptions.correct: String Pool is also subject to garbage collection (GC).
misconceptions.why: Before Java 7, there was a memory shortage problem in the PermGen area, but starting from Java 7, it is moved to the general Heap and is automatically cleaned if there are no references.

keyTakeaway: Literals are reused in Pool, and new always creates a new object. Comparison is done with .equals()!
